summary: Documents the interface for the IBM 5250 Telnet implementation, which lets 5250-style terminals be used over TCP/IP. It is informational and describes an existing implementation, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Some old IBM screens spoke their own language. This explains how to use them over the Internet.

subtitle: How a Telnet client can emulate an IBM 5250 work station, down to the record header on every screen.

tldr.problem: IBM 5250 work stations speak their own data stream, and hosts on the Internet that wanted to support them over Telnet had no written description of the interface.
tldr.mechanism: Client and server agree on the Binary, End-Of-Record and Terminal-Type Telnet options, then exchange 5250 data prefixed by a small header and ended by IAC EOR. The memo also lists corrections and additions to IBM's 5250 manual.
tldr.outcome: The memo is informational and defines no standard. It documents an existing IBM implementation, and RFC 2877 later updated it.

today: RFC 1205 is an Informational RFC and is not a standard. It has been updated by RFC 2877.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 1205 describes the interface to the IBM 5250 Telnet implementation. Its goal is to let someone write a client Telnet that emulates an IBM 5250 work station.

It does not cover every 5250 command or aid code. Those are in IBM's 5250 Information Display System, Functions Reference Manual (SA21-9247). Corrections and additions to that manual are collected in section 5 of the RFC. The memo says plainly that it does not specify any standard.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a how-to for making a computer pretend to be a certain kind of old IBM screen over the Internet.

sections.title: Telnet Options and Terminal Types
sections.content:
No new Telnet options are defined. To enter 5250 mode, client and server must both agree to support at least the Binary, End-Of-Record (EOR) and Terminal-Type options. The terminal type names the screen the client emulates, for example IBM-5251-11 (24 x 80 monochrome) or IBM-3477-FC (27 x 132 color). The full list is kept in the Assigned Numbers RFC.

In the RFC's example, the server sends DO TERMINAL-TYPE, asks for the type, and the client answers. Then both sides agree to send EOR and to use binary transmission, each in both directions.
sections.plainLanguage: Before talking, both sides agree on the rules and the client says which model of screen it is pretending to be.

sections.title: The Record Header
sections.content:
Each record is a header followed by the 5250 data stream. The header was originally designed for 5250 Display Station Pass-Through (DSPT) on the AS/400, System/36 and System/38. It has a fixed part of 6 octets and a variable part, which is currently always 4 octets.

The fixed part holds the Logical Record Length (including the header, counted before any IAC doubling, and not counting the trailing IAC EOR), the Record Type (always 12A0 hex, the General Data Stream) and 16 reserved bits.

The variable part holds the length of that part (04 hex), a 16-bit flags field and an 8-bit opcode. The flags include ERR (output error), ATN (attention key), SRQ (System Request key), TRQ (Test Request key) and HLP (Help in Error State). The opcodes include No Operation (00), Put/Get (03), Save Screen (04), Restore Screen (05) and Cancel Invite (0A). The record ends with IAC EOR, and some operations are just a header with no data stream.

Example: 000A 12A0 0000 0400 000B FFEF is a Turn On Message Light request, 10 octets long, with no flags set.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message wears a label. The label says how long the message is, what kind it is, and what to do with it, such as turn the message light on.

sections.title: Data Flow Examples
sections.content:
The RFC shows hex dumps for three common flows. In the Query example the server sends a Write Structured Field Query command and the client must answer with a Query Reply describing its capabilities. In the Cancel Invite example the server reverses the normal direction of flow, and the client replies with its own Cancel Invite and sends no user data until the server invites the work station again.

In the System Request example the client sets the SRQ flag. The server then cancels the invite, saves the screen, sends the System Request menu, takes the user's input, restores the saved screen and finally sends a Read MDT command to invite the work station again.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples are like scripts of a phone call: who speaks first, who answers, and how they hand the turn back and forth.

sections.title: Additions to the 5250 Data Stream
sections.content:
Section 5 works as an addendum to IBM manual SA21-9247-6. It fixes errors: the Insert Cursor order is listed as hex 03 but the correct value is hex 13. It also adds features:

  • A flag in the Write to Display control character that decides whether the cursor moves at the end of processing.
  • A transparent field (Field Control Word 84xx hex), whose contents are sent to the host unformatted, so any value from hex 00 to FF is allowed.
  • New commands: Read MDT Fields Alternate (82) and Read MDT Fields Immediate Alternate (83).
  • New orders: Move Cursor (14) and Transparent Data (10).
  • A Query command and a Query Reply that reports controller class, device type, keyboard, screen size, color and other capabilities.

The memo states that security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: The note also fixes typos in IBM's manual and adds a few new buttons, like moving the cursor anywhere or asking the screen what it can do.

messages.label: SB TERMINAL-TYPE IS IBM-5251-11
messages.note: The client names the screen it emulates.

messages.label: IAC DO END-OF-RECORD
messages.note: The server and client then both agree to EOR, and likewise to TRANSMIT-BINARY.
